title: asymmetric-routing-detect-and-dive-notes
content:
Goal: collect a concise breadcrumbs-style log of steps/commands tried while investigating an intermittent TLS handshake reset for private-deploy customers across a peered VPC path. Keep raw outputs and hypotheses in one place to hand off to SRE/Networking and the customer SE.

Summary of problem:
- Symptom: TLS connections from customer app in customer-VPC -> service in provider-VPC intermittently fail with TCP RST from intermediate hop after ServerHello (server sees client, but SSL_read on customer side gets RST). Failures ~1-2% of connections, correlate with larger payloads and slower RTTs.
- Affects: private deployments using VPC peering + cross-account routing in region-us-west-2.
- Hypothesis: asymmetric routing / intermediate NAT device or egress gateway dropping/rewriting packets, causing state mismatch (conntrack) and TLS teardown. Possible MTU/MSS/clamping or path that returns via different IGW/Transitgateway than forward.

Timeline / key observations:
- 2024-10-15: First customer report (latency + occasional TLS resets).
- 2024-10-17: Reproduced from inside customer pod (kubectl exec) with curl -v to service IP: observed reset after ServerHello on ~1/20 attempts.
- 2024-10-21: Ran tcpdump on both sides; saw SYN->SYN/ACK->ACK flow, ClientHello -> ServerHello -> [RST from 172.31.12.5]. That IP is a transit NAT IP in partner account.
- 2024-10-25: Notified partner infra, they saw same IP in flow logs, but no anomaly on their instance metrics.

Commands tried (copied outputs trimmed, timestamps present):
1) traceroute (from customer pod to service VIP)
$ traceroute -n -w 1 -q 1 10.200.5.18
traceroute to 10.200.5.18 (10.200.5.18), 30 hops max, 60 byte packets
 1  10.0.3.1  0.16 ms
 2  172.16.8.2  0.43 ms
 3  172.31.12.5  1.12 ms   <-- transit NAT hop seen in tcpdump
 4  10.200.5.18  1.38 ms

2) Simple curl showing failure pattern (inside customer pod):
$ curl -v --resolve service.example.internal:443:10.200.5.18 https://service.example.internal/health --http1.1 -m 5
* Connected to 10.200.5.18 (10.200.5.18) port 443 (#0)
* ALPN, offering http/1.1
* TLS 1.3 connection using TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256
* TLS: Server certificate OK
* Using HTTP1.1
* Mark bundle as not supporting multiuse
> GET /health HTTP/1.1
> Host: service.example.internal
> User-Agent: curl/7.68.0
> Accept: */*
* Connection #0 to host 10.200.5.18 left intact
* Empty reply from server
* Closing connection 0

Note: sometimes curl shows "Empty reply from server" which is consistent with a TCP RST after handshake.

3) openssl s_client with verbose and showcerts
$ openssl s_client -connect 10.200.5.18:443 -servername service.example.internal -msg -tlsextdebug -status
... (handshake trace) ...
<<< TLS 1.3, Handshake [length 0004]
    16 03 03 00 85 ... ServerHello ...
*** (1.10 seconds later) ***
write:errno=104
errno=104 -> Connection reset by peer

4) tcpdump (customer side) capturing from pod veth interface (filter host 10.200.5.18):
15:22:04.123456 IP 10.0.5.23.52014 > 10.200.5.18.443: Flags [S], seq 12345, win 64240, options [mss 1420,sackOK,TS val 123456 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7], length 0
15:22:04.123457 IP 10.200.5.18.443 > 10.0.5.23.52014: Flags [S.], seq 654321, ack 12346, win 28960, options [mss 1400,sackOK,TS val 654321 ecr 123456], length 0
15:22:04.123458 IP 10.0.5.23.52014 > 10.200.5.18.443: Flags [.], ack 1, win 502, options [nop,nop,TS val 123457 ecr 654321], length 0
15:22:04.124912 IP 10.0.5.23.52014 > 10.200.5.18.443: Flags [P.], seq 1:520, ack 1, win 502, length 519
15:22:04.125023 IP 10.200.5.18.443 > 10.0.5.23.52014: Flags [.], ack 520, win 28960, length 0
15:22:04.226000 IP 172.31.12.5.40012 > 10.0.5.23.52014: Flags [R], seq 99, win 0, length 0   <-- reset observed from transit IP

Observation: RST originates from 172.31.12.5 (not the server). Server did send ACK earlier. That suggests an intermediate device is closing the forward state or returning a forged RST.

5) conntrack dump on host (customer side)
$ sudo conntrack -L | grep 10.0.5.23 | grep 10.200.5.18 -m 5
tcp      6 431999 ESTABLISHED src=10.0.5.23 dst=10.200.5.18 sport=52014 dport=443 src=10.200.5.18 dst=10.0.5.23 sport=443 dport=52014 [ASSURED] mark=0 use=1

6) iptables/nat rules quick inspection
$ sudo iptables -t nat -S
(no relevant NAT rules)

7) dmesg / kernel drops around time of repro (host kernel log)
Oct 21 15:22:04 host kernel: NETDEV WATCHDOG: eth0 (vxlan0): transmit timed out
Oct 21 15:22:04 host kernel: device eth0 entered promiscuous mode
(not conclusive)

8) netcat between endpoints (to test large payloads and fragmentation)
- stream of 64k bytes triggers earlier reset frequency -> suspicion: path MTU or middlebox with small buffer.

Hypotheses and reasoning:
- H1: Asymmetric return path via partner NAT device that does not see initial SYN (or has stale conntrack entry) and mistakes the TLS application payload for an unsolicited packet, responding with RST. Evidence: RST source != server IP.
- H2: MTU / fragmentation issue leading to middlebox mis-parsing TLS records and injecting RST when seeing a fragmented record boundary. Evidence: resets correlate with larger request body sizes and traces show varied MSS values at hop 3.
- H3: Conntrack table overflow on the transit host occasionally evicts entries; subsequent packets trigger RST. Evidence: occasional 'conntrack: table full' seen in partner logs (reported by partner).
- H4: Stateful firewall/IPS in partner path is treating HTTP/1.1 keepalive frames with POST body as suspicious; drops or resets. Less likely but needs to be ruled out.

Tests to run next (owned or suggested):
- A: Reproduce with varied MSS: force curl --interface to set small MTU / use iptables TOS or iproute2 to set PMTU hints. Collect pcap on both sides.
- B: Run identical test with source port pinned vs ephemeral to see if NAT sticky mapping changes behaviour (script that reuses same source port).
- C: Partner: enable detailed conntrack logging (drop/evict events) around repro window.
- D: Ask partner to mirror traffic to a VM for deep inspection (tcpdump) and to capture details for packets with seq numbers in logs.
- E: Try flaky path mitigation: enable TCP MSS clamping on customer-side NAT/egress and observe.
- F: Run synthetics from multiple AZs to see whether return path changes (if asymmetry is region/AZ-specific).

Quick reproducer script (local pod):
for i in $(seq 1 100); do 
  curl -sS -w "%{http_code} %{time_connect} %{time_starttransfer}\n" --resolve service.example.internal:443:10.200.5.18 \
    -H "Content-Type: application/octet-stream" --data-binary "$(head -c $((1024 + (RANDOM % 65500))) /dev/urandom | base64)" https://service.example.internal/health || echo "curl-fail-$i";
  sleep 0.5;
done
Record stderr stdout to /tmp/repro-<ts>.log and capture tcpdump concurrently: sudo tcpdump -i any host 10.200.5.18 -w /tmp/pcap-<ts>.pcap

Notes for handoff to partner SRE:
- Provide server-side packet captures around the same timestamps; include TCP seq/ack numbers so we can correlate which side sent which packet leading to reset.
- Share conntrack dumps pre/post repro and dmesg.
- Ask partner to search for "conntrack: table full" or Any kernel logs about nf_conntrack evictions.
- If partner uses a transit appliance (NGFW), request policy log around those timestamps for any session teardown events.

Temporary mitigation idea:
- If MSS/clamping resolves flakiness in quick tests, document procedure to enable on egress NAT gateway for affected subnets. Rollout low-risk patch to subset of customers and monitor.

Useful references and prior incidents:
- Link to RI-2345 (investigation ticket) includes partner flow logs and initial pcap snippets.
- CONFLUENCE-9876: internal writeup on private-deploy routing and peering patterns (useful to understand route propagation order).

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why does RST appear to be from correct autonomous hop IP (172.31.12.5) rather than random forged IP? Is that device purposely sending RST or is it observing a burst and resetting?
- Does NAT on partner change source port mapping mid-flow (e.g., due to ephemeral port reuse) which could invalidate conntrack entry?
- Any middlebox with TLS-aware deep packet inspection that might inject resets on seeing specific record patterns?

Next notes (short log of actions):
- 2024-11-02: Added MSS clamping on local host (net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing=1) for quick test. Small improvement: failure rate dropped from 1.8% -> 0.6% in 5k requests.
- 2024-11-05: Partner reported seeing repeated SYN from same source ports but 50% of those flows had no matching conntrack entry on transit device.
- 2024-12-01: Partner upgraded NGFW firmware; new logs show "session lookup failed" entries correlating with our timestamps.

If handing off, include this file plus /tmp/pcap-* and repro logs. Tag ticket RI-2345 and request a joint debug call with partner networking in the same time window when a repro is being executed.

Personal TODO (Samir):
- Add script to correlate tcpdump seq/ack numbers with conntrack entries automatically.
- Run controlled repro with only SYN/ACK/PSH sizes that trigger failures to further narrow MTU vs state issue.
- Draft a short mitigation playbook (MSS clamp + route fallback) for customer-facing runbook if partner-side fix delayed.

End of scratchpad.
